questions.stem: The two-way table shows students' favourite sport by gender. How many more girls than boys prefer netball?
questions.hint: Find the netball values for boys and girls, then subtract.

steps.explain: Read off the number of girls and boys who prefer netball.

questions.stem: A dot plot shows the number of pets owned by 15 students: 0 pets — 3 students, 1 pet — 6 students, 2 pets — 4 students, 3 pets — 2 students. What is the mode of this data?
options: \(1\text{ pet}\)
\(0\text{ pets}\)
\(6\text{ pets}\)
\(15\text{ pets}\)
questions.hint: The mode is the value that occurs most often.

steps.explain: Compare the number of students for each value: 3, 6, 4, 2.
steps.work: The highest count is 6, for "1 pet"

steps.explain: The mode is the pet count with the highest frequency, not the frequency itself.

questions.stem: A line graph records temperature through the day: 6am — \(10°\text{C}\), 9am — \(14°\text{C}\), 12pm — \(22°\text{C}\), 3pm — \(25°\text{C}\), 6pm — \(19°\text{C}\). What is the range of temperatures recorded?

steps.explain: Identify the highest and lowest recorded temperatures.

questions.stem: A bar graph's vertical axis starts at \(50\) instead of \(0\), as shown. What effect does this have on how the bars appear?
options: It makes the difference between the bars look much bigger than it really is
It makes the difference between the bars look smaller than it really is
It has no effect on how the bars look
It makes both bars look identical
questions.hint: Compare the true difference (65−55=10) to how large that difference LOOKS when the axis is cut off at 50 rather than starting at 0.

steps.explain: The true difference between the two values is only 10 (65 − 55).
But because the axis starts at 50 (not 0), that difference of 10 takes up a much larger share of the visible bar heights than it should.
steps.work: Truncating the axis exaggerates the visual difference

questions.stem: A pie chart shows the favourite fruit of a class: Apples \(40\%\), Bananas \(35\%\), Oranges \(35\%\). What is wrong with this pie chart?
options: The percentages add up to more than \(100\%\), which is impossible for a whole pie chart
Pie charts cannot show fruit data
There are too few categories
Nothing is wrong with it
questions.hint: Add up all the percentages shown.

steps.explain: A complete pie chart must represent exactly \(100\%\) — this one is inaccurate.

questions.stem: An online poll on a video-game website asks visitors "Do you play video games daily?" and finds that \(95\%\) said yes. Why might this result be misleading if used to describe the general population?
options: The people surveyed were already visitors to a gaming website, so they are not a representative sample of everyone
95% is too high a number to be measured accurately
Online polls can never be about video games
The question was too short
questions.hint: Think about who would be visiting a gaming website in the first place.

steps.explain: The sample (visitors to a gaming website) is heavily biased toward people who are already interested in gaming.
steps.work: Sample is not representative of the wider population

steps.explain: This is called sampling bias — the result cannot be generalised beyond that specific group.
steps.work: The 95% figure overstates video-game habits in the general population

questions.stem: A graph in a news article shows that both ice-cream sales and shark attacks increase during summer months. Does this mean ice-cream sales cause shark attacks?
options: No — both are likely caused by a third factor (warm weather leads to more swimming and more ice-cream eating)
Yes — the graph proves ice-cream causes shark attacks
Yes, but only in coastal towns
No, because sharks do not eat ice-cream
questions.hint: Two things happening at the same time (correlation) does not mean one causes the other.

steps.explain: Both ice-cream sales and shark attacks rise in warm weather, but for unrelated reasons — more people swim, and more people buy ice-cream.
steps.work: Warm weather is the common underlying cause of both

steps.explain: This is an example of correlation without causation.
steps.work: Ice-cream does not cause shark attacks
